ImageDescription.value:
cueva de la pileta It's a hike, both to get to the cave, and once inside, as well, but there's a handrail and steps carved in almost the whole way. Bring plenty of cash, be prepared to wait for a group to form, wear the least slippery shoes you have, and gloves if you think you might want to carry a lantern, don't bring a flashlight, don't let anyone see your camera, and use only passive-type night-vision.

As with most caves that you have to pay to get inside, it's a "trip" - but this one has real, truly visible paleolithic cave art, even in the portions of the cave that are not closed-off from tourists.

ImageDescription.value:
Lava continues to flow from Mauna Loa just outside the boundaries of Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park, a few miles east of Pu'u 'O'o.

From 5:00pm until 8:00pm, visitors can drive over a lava covered highway, to a section of roadway that is still clear to park. Everyone must back into your parking spot, incase a quick getaway is in order - no joke. You then make the 15 minute hike over an old flow, to a roped off viewing area to see lava pour into the ocean at night.

The viewing area is roped off for your own safety. In November of 2005, 35 acres of shoreline (the 'lava bench') collapsed into the ocean. About 10 years before that, a similar collapse occurred. It is wise to stay within the roped off area.

It's quite a spectacular experience, but be aware that your hike back will be in complete darkness, over very sharp, hardened black lava. The park rangers organising the viewing say people get hurt every single night, without fail. Be prepared with your flashlight, decent hiking shoes, water and some common sense. It's a spectacular sight.

If you are exceptionally brave, you can take a 'lava boat' ride, which brings you within a few hundred feet of the hot lava flowing into the ocean. Note the 'lava boat' in the bottom left of this picture.

We opted for the hike.

72720788.title: File:Hikers gather near the water during the early moments of the fire. Photo courtesy of Noah Brown. (38704677035).jpg

ObjectName.value: Hikers gather near the water during the early moments of the fire. Photo courtesy of Noah Brown. (38704677035)

Categories.value: PD US USDA FS|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|USFS files uploaded by Tyler de Noche|People at Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area|Files from the U.S. Forest Service Pacific Northwest Region Flickr stream

ImageDescription.value:
The Eagle Creek Fire ignited on Saturday, September 2nd 2017. Approximately 150 people were on the Eagle Creek Trail when the fire erupted.

Dozens and dozens of hikers began to congregate at Punch Bowl Falls as they began to weigh their options and to decide what to do next. Overhead a helicopter dropped a canister to the group that contained two notes. The first said the fire was growing fast and that everybody needed to start heading down toward the Columbia River. The second said to ignore the first message; that we can see you and to stay put. The second note said DANGER.

With the rapidly growing fire now blocking their path to the trailhead, it was decided that the best course of action would be for the group to head further up the trail to meet up with rescue personnel who could then escort them out to safety. After hiking 11 miles Sharon Steriti, Trail Crew Leader from the Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument, was the first person to reach the group. Dressed in her Forest Service uniform, she was a welcome sight for the weary group where she set about to instantly put them at ease by handing out food and supplies.

Guided by the glow of smartphones, headlamps and flashlights, Sharon led the group of 143 people and two dogs just past Tunnel Falls, where they would stop to rest for the night.

Later in the night another group of rescuers would arrive, and with extra food and emergency supplies. The group was ready to get moving with the first light of dawn. Their destination was 7.5 miles up the trail at Wahtum Lake, where school buses and rescue personnel were waiting for them. By mid-afternoon everyone had successfully walked out to the trailhead.

The Sierra Madre News is the longest, continuous running newspaper in the City of Sierra Madre. It was published from October 1906 to June 1999. The newspaper was published by R. T. Cowles and yearly subscriptions cost $1.50. Successive editors include: C.W. Hill, George Morgridge, L.R. Goshorn. Clifford C. Ward, Peter Ward, Edgar W. Jenkinson, William F. Thomas, Ed E. Herwig, R. Robert Evans, Jannene G. Reed, and Michael De Wees. The paper was printed with a hand press, and then a two-revolution cylinder press, and starting in 1947 a 52-inch Miehle flat bed double revolution press, and finally using the offset method.
For additional information see California Revealed.

ImageDescription.value:
The mist felt magical, as if I was on the edge of heaven and my recently departed mom was looking over me.

A little further along, I got lost and did an extra two miles that ended at a dead end trail overlook. On the way back, I filtered water out of a livestock trough and then walked through a gate back towards the way I should have come. Taking my compas out, I convinced myself after hiking up a small but steep hill, that I needed to turn around and head the other way. When I went back through the gate, I consulted my AllTrails app instructions and found my way past a little park and back onto the trail.

A little further along the trail, I met Joshua, Justin and Lee who were also headed towards Black Jack Campground. They told me that the ranger said the trail was closed and we all scoffed at the idea and continued on. This was a nice section of single track trail, one of the few as most of the trail is dirt roads. Eventually I got to a part where the mud started to clod up on my shoes until I felt like a drag queen on platform shoes in a nightmare. I opted to turn right and walk the next three miles on the road rather than slogging it through the mud. Josh, Justin and Lee apparently opted to do the same.

As I walked along the road to the airport, the blisters were really starting to take a toll on me. A friendly eco-tour guide drove along beside me for a bit with her open Jeep and passengers and chatted me up. "I hope you have some plastic," she said. "I'm all set, I've got a tent," I replied. I asked where the turn for Black jack was and she said there was a bus stop three miles up the road and to turn left there. Then it was another mile in. This disappointed me as I thought I only had three miles to go but now it turned out it would be four. Then when I got to the bus stop, it was actually 1.3 miles to Black Jack Campground so with the blisters clamoring for my attention, this day just did not seem to want to end.

Eventually, I pulled into camp and set up my tent before dark and the rain. Joshua, Justin and Lee pulled into camp in the dark. I waved my key fob flashlight in the air to welcome them.

The next morning, I saw that the guys had set up their two tents right at the end of the road and subjected themselves to a river of mud during the night. Lee said it felt like he was sleeping on a water bed because there was two inches of water under his tent that was floating. The waterproof floor comes up to four inches luckily so the water only leaked in once when Lee accidentally pressed down a little to close to the edge.
